Beállítom Magyar kötődésű startuppal kezd hivatalos együttműködésbe a tőzsdei bevezetésre készülő mesterségesintelligencia-cég, az Anthropic. A Claude pénzügyi tanácsadóknak kifejlesztett verziójában ugyanis a budapesti székhelyű magyar-amerikai Zocks virtuális asszisztenséhez férhetnek majd hozzá a felhasználók, közölte a startup a Telexszel, miután hétfőn bemutatták az Anthropic fejlesztését Kaliforniában . A 2022-ben alapított Zocks elsősorban pénzügyi cégek, tanácsadók és vagyonkezelők számára fejlesztenek az adatvédelmet előtérbe helyező mesterséges intelligencia alapú asszisztenst. Az asszisztens meglehetősen gyorsabbá és hatékonyabbá teszi a munkavégzést: automatizálja a korábban manuálisan végzett feladatokat, jegyzetel, minden ügyfélbeszélgetést, emaileket és dokumentumokat strukturált adattá alakít, így ezek könnyebben kereshetővé válnak, emlékeztetőket küld. A most beharangozott fejlesztés azt jelenti, hogy a Zockson keresztül a Claude megkapja majd a teljes kontextust, a valós ügyféladatokat, az ügyfél által megosztott terveket, prioritásokat, aggodalmakat, a tanácsadóknak nem kell nagyon részletes promptokat írniuk, összességében így jóval hatékonyabban fog tudni feladatokat végrehajtani a Claude. A startup a Forbes 2025-ös A legforróbb magyar startupok listáján az ötödik helyen végzett, akkor azt írták a Zocks termékéről, hogy hatszor-hétszer drágább az átlagos versenytársaknál, emiatt célozták meg elsősorban a pénzügyi szektort, ugyanis ott kevésbé árérzékenyek a cégek. A cég vezetői ugyanekkor azt is mondták, hangsúlyosan az amerikai piacot célozták meg, budapesti irodájukban a fejlesztői csapatot építik. A startupnak Budapest mellett San Franciscóban van irodája, alapítói Ratku Ákos és Mark Gilbert. Az Anthropic jelenleg a világ egyik legdinamikusabban fejlődő és legfelkapottabb techcége, becsült értéke májusban 965 milliárd dollár volt, jelenleg IPO-ra készül, ami heteken belül meg is történhet. Szeptember elején viszont összecsaptak a hullámok a cég feje fölött, miután az Anthropic egykori kutatója arról posztolt az X-en, hogy az MI-fejlesztés jelenlegi versenye komoly veszélyt jelenthet az emberiségre. Pár napra rá a cég közzétett egy fenyegetés-elemző jelentést, amiben részletesen leírta, hogy több piaci szereplő is felhasználta a Claude-ot a fegyverfejlesztéstől és a kiberoperációktól a megfigyelésig és a csalásig bezárólag. Dario Amodei, az Anthropic vezérigazgatója később felszólította a mesterséges intelligencia területén működő vállalatokat, hogy lassítsák a modellek képességeinek fejlesztési ütemét, tekintettel a mesterséges intelligencia visszaélésszerű használatával kapcsolatos egyre növekvő aggodalmakra. „A fejlődés így is gyorsnak fog tűnni, és bölcsen kell felhasználnunk a nyert időt” – írta Amodei egy esszében , amit az X-en osztott meg. Az Economist szerint egyébként a lassítás önmagában nem feltétlenül lenne rossz üzletileg az Anthropicnak, mivel a cég bevételének nagy részét adó vállalati ügyfelek számára a jelenlegi modellek már most is elég intelligensek. Azaz az MI-modellek további gyors fejlesztése nem feltétlenül szükséges ahhoz, hogy a vállalat tovább növelje a bevételét. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! https://exclaim.ca/film/article/tiff-202.text: TIFF 2026: 'Fjord' Thrives in Ambiguity Directed by Cristian Mungiu Starring Sebastian Stan, Renate Reinsve Photo courtesy of Elevation Pictures BY Rachel Ho Published Sep 10, 2026 7 Cristian Mungiu 's Fjord presents an interesting question in a world where liberal and conservative values have construction firm boundaries: to what end should freedom be afforded to us? Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve play the parents of the Gheorghiu family, both turning in powerful performances. Stan's Mihai met Reinsve's Lisbet in his home country of Romania where his soon-to-be Norwegian wife was visiting, and the two got married, had five children and are raising them in a strict, traditional, conservative, religious — whichever adjective you'd like to ascribe to them — household. When the family decides to move from Romania to Lisbet's native, and generally left-leaning, Norway, the Gheorghius find themselves going against the grain of their local village. Their outward devotion to prayer and religious study flies in the face of the agnostic approach to religion their neighbours prefer. Even their sense of dress, especially Lisbet and her daughters, seems out of time. But these are all differences that have only warranted whispered judgments. It isn't until their eldest daughter arrives to school with some bruising that those in positions of authority begin to intrude in on the family's way of life. Fjord carries echoes of Anatomy of a Fall , the French courtroom drama that garnered North American interest, but without the prior film's whodunnit mystery. Mihai and Lisbet both admit to disciplining their children with physical force, namely slaps to the hands and behind; however, they insist that this does not amount to abuse. It's this point of difference that gives Fjord its on-screen drama and off-screen discourse. Writer-director Mungiu creates a circular argument that lends Mihai and Lisbet, and in turn their right-leaning ideals, sympathy to a degree that some audiences will find uncomfortable, and I'd wager that's entirely Mungiu's intention. Fjord doesn't provide any easy or satisfying answers, but they're not ambiguous either. The most interesting element of Fjord , though, comes from the unspoken tension between Western and Eastern Europe, and the perception of migrants from a country like Romania to a country like Norway. Mungiu doesn't press upon this divide too overtly, although it's clear nonetheless and only enriches the inevitable discussion post-movie. Fjord ends on the cinematic equivalent of hanging punctuation — it aligns the entire story appropriately, yet feels like we're breaking from the family mid-sentence, which in many ways gives the film its edge and brilliance. The 2026 Toronto International Film Festival runs from September 10 to 20 in Toronto. Find details and ticket information at the festival's website. https://www.dw.com/en/saudi-arabia-secon.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O802 Riyadh airport will be closed until at least Sunday night [FILE: 2019] Image: Valery Sharifulin/TASS/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia , was struck by an "unidentified projectile" for the second time in two days on Sunday, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen . "King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was subjected to a new attack on Sunday afternoon," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement, adding that it "resulted in injuries, and the assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities are still under way." Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki also said that a cruise missile had been intercepted by air defense systems in the vicinity of the airport, but no further details were immediately available. The Houthis later claimed responsibility for the strikes, saying they had "carried out four qualitative operations in the past 24 hours using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones." A spokesman said the group targeted the Riyadh airport multiple times, as well as the Dammam airport and two facilities belonging to the Saudi state oil company Aramco. Sunday's strikes came as Riyadh airport remained closed following an attack on Saturday which killed 12 people and injured over 300 more — the deadliest such strike on the kingdom in over a decade. On Sunday, the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia confirmed that one of its citizens died after being wounded in Saturday's attack. "It is learnt that one Indian national injured in the Riyadh attack has unfortunately lost his life today," read a statement posted on social media. "We convey our heartfelt condolences to the family of the deceased." Houthis warn airlines after deadly Riyadh airport strike To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Houthis warn airlines to avoid Saudi Arabia It also came just hours after the Houthis warned airlines and travelers to avoid Saudi airports. "We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our forces," read a statement released by the group on social media. It added that airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina would not be targeted. "We ‌urge everyone to take our warnings seriously," the statement continued, stating: "Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions." What now for Saudi Arabia after Riyadh airport attack? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Why are Saudi airports being targeted? Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the rebels seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, including around the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthi-run health authority claimed this weekend that 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in the last five weeks, 60% of them women and children. Earlier on Sunday, it said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa. The Houthi-run Al Masirah TV also reported that Saudi Arabia had struck the international airport in Sanaa on Sunday afternoon. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims. "Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the Houthi-run Foreign Ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah TV on Sunday, adding that its ​actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity. What has Saudi Arabia said about the Riyadh airport attacks? The Saudi-led coalition, which supports the internationally recognized Yemeni government in its conflict against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, vowed a tough response to the attack, which it labeled a "full-fledged war crime." The Houthi strikes on Riyadh come amid a surge in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia this week, which have targeted other airports, military sites and oil infrastructure. The spike in attacks has followed a major military offensive by the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis. The rebels, one of Tehran's regional proxies , have been fighting Yemen's government, which is recognized by the international community, since the outbreak of a civil war over a decade ago. While a truce in 2022 froze the conflict, it failed to secure a lasting peace deal. The US-Israeli war with Iran has seen fighting flare up again in Yemen, worsening an already severe humanitarian crisis . Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video How has the international community reacted to the Riyadh strikes? US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he would be speaking to Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in the wake of the attack, which he said was "not acceptable." Trump also said that the US was "going to look" at potentially joining Saudi strikes against the rebels. On Sunday, European leaders expressed their "shock" at the attack on Riyadh airport. The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia" as she condemned the "dangerous escalation." "These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shock waves sent through the world," von der Leyen said. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul "firmly" condemned what he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation". "Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he said on X. UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting slammed the attacks as "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation," while the French Foreign Ministry condemned the "heinous attack" and stressed its "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia. Russia, which is a strategic partner of Iran, also condemned the Houthis' attack and called for the hostilities to end "through political and diplomatic means." Australia, meanwhile, has urged its citizens in the Saudi capital to "shelter in place" amid the escalating attacks. Why can't the Saudis defeat the Houthis?
